subject: chem
title: C2 – Chemical Calculations
outcomesHtml:
The candidate is able to do calculations on a process, using knowledge of chemical reactions and laws of conservation.

  1. The candidate is able to use the following concepts in calculations:
    • mass: symbol m, unit kg
    • volume: symbol V, unit m³
    • relative molecular mass: symbol Mr
    • chemical quantity: symbol n(X), unit mol
    • molar mass: symbol M(X), unit g mol⁻¹
    • molar volume: symbol Vm, unit m³ mol⁻¹
    • density: symbol ρ, unit kg m⁻³
    • concentration: symbol c(X), [X], unit mol L⁻¹
    • mass percentage: unit %
    • mass-ppm: unit ppm, mg kg⁻¹
    • mass-ppb: unit ppb, μg kg⁻¹
    • volume percentage: unit %
    • acidity: symbol pH
      • pH = −log [H⁺]; pH = −log [H₃O⁺]
      • pOH = −log [OH⁻]
      • pH + pOH = 14.00 (at 298 K)
      • [H⁺] = 10−pH; [H₃O⁺] = 10−pH
      • [OH⁻] = 10−pOH
  2. The candidate is able to use the following principles in calculations on and descriptions of chemical processes:
    • mass ratio
    • volume ratio of gases in reactions
    • excess/deficiency
    • stoichiometric ratio
    • yield as a fraction or percentage of the theoretical output.
notesHtml:
C2 — Chemical calculations: notes

Status: checked against the CCVX syllabus and Binas (5th edition or later). All worked examples in these notes are original. Practice questions with full solutions are in practice.md.

These notes cover the two CCVX learning outcomes: the quantities used in calculations (C2.1) and the principles behind process calculations (C2.2). Data come from Binas; since table numbers differ between editions, tables are named. Binas is allowed in the exam, so practise finding every value you use.

C2.1 Quantities

Amount of substance and molar mass

  • The amount of substance, symbol n(X), is counted in mol (CCVX calls it the chemical quantity). One mole contains 6.022·10²³ particles, the Avogadro constant N_A (Binas, table of fundamental constants). So N = n × N_A.
  • The molar mass M(X) in g mol⁻¹ has the same number as the molecular mass in u: H₂O is 18.02 u and M(H₂O) = 18.02 g mol⁻¹. Take molar masses from the Binas table of molar masses, or add up atomic masses from the table of atomic masses (H 1.008, C 12.01, O 16.00, and so on).
  • The central conversion is n = m / M, with m in g. If a mass is given in kg, mg or tonnes, convert to grams first.
  • CCVX also names the relative molecular mass M_r, a unit-free number. It equals the molar-mass number.

Worked example (original). How many molecules are in 9.00 g of water?

  1. M(H₂O) = 2 × 1.008 + 16.00 = 18.02 g mol⁻¹ (Binas).
  2. n = m / M = 9.00 / 18.02 = 0.499 mol.
  3. N = n × N_A = 0.499 × 6.022·10²³ = 3.01·10²³ molecules.

More conversions of this type: practice chem-c02-q01.

Concentration and molarity

  • Concentration c(X) or [X] = n / V, in mol L⁻¹. The number of moles per litre is also called the molarity; “0.100 M” means 0.100 mol L⁻¹.
  • Solutions of ionic compounds need care: one formula unit can give several particles. In 0.25 M Na₂SO₄, [Na⁺] = 0.50 mol L⁻¹ and [SO₄²⁻] = 0.25 mol L⁻¹. See chem-c02-q02.
  • Diluting keeps n constant, so c₁V₁ = c₂V₂.
  • At the equivalence point of a titration, the amounts of the two reactants stand in the ratio of the reaction equation. A known volume and concentration on one side then give the unknown concentration on the other.

Worked example (original). A 20.00 mL sample of hydrochloric acid is titrated with 0.1050 M sodium hydroxide. The equivalence point is reached after 19.04 mL. Calculate the molarity of the acid.

  1. Reaction: H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ → 2 H₂O, so at the equivalence point n(H₃O⁺) = n(OH⁻).
  2. n(NaOH) = 0.1050 mol L⁻¹ × 19.04·10⁻³ L = 1.999·10⁻³ mol.
  3. c(HCl) = 1.999·10⁻³ mol / 20.00·10⁻³ L = 0.09996 mol L⁻¹ ≈ 0.1000 M.

Titrations: chem-c02-q08; back-titrations: chem-c02-q09.

Density

  • ρ = m / V. Useful conversions: 1 kg m⁻³ = 1 g L⁻¹ = 10⁻³ g mL⁻¹. Most mistakes happen in this unit conversion, so always write the units in every step.
  • The Binas gas-density table applies at 273 K and p = p₀ only. For other conditions, the question gives the density.

Worked example (original). Ethanol has density 0.789 g mL⁻¹. What amount of ethanol (C₂H₆O, M = 46.07 g mol⁻¹) is in a 25.0 mL measuring cylinder?

  1. m = ρ × V = 0.789 × 25.0 = 19.7 g.
  2. n = m / M = 19.7 / 46.07 = 0.428 mol.

Density and percentage combined (concentrated acids): chem-c02-q12.

Molar volume of gases

  • V_m = V / n. Its value depends on temperature and pressure but not on the gas: every gas behaves the same (Avogadro's law).
  • Values from Binas (table of fundamental constants): V_m = 22.4 L mol⁻¹ at 273 K and 24.5 L mol⁻¹ at 298 K, both at p = p₀.
  • Unless a question says otherwise, assume T = 298 K and p = p₀, so V = n × 24.5 L.

Worked example (original). Calculate the volume of 0.200 mol of carbon dioxide at 298 K and p = p₀.

  1. V = n × V_m = 0.200 × 24.5 = 4.90 L.

Gas calculations: chem-c02-q06, chem-c02-q13.

Percentages, ppm and ppb

  • Mass percentage = m(part) / m(total) × 100%. Volume percentage = V(part) / V(total) × 100%. For example, chlorine in PVC (C₂H₃Cl repeated unit, M_r = 62.49): 35.45 / 62.49 × 100% = 56.73%.
  • ppm (parts per million) is the same fraction × 10⁶; ppb × 10⁹. CCVX gives the units directly: mass-ppm is mg kg⁻¹, mass-ppb is μg kg⁻¹, volume-ppm is cm³ m⁻³.
  • For dilute water samples, 1 L ≈ 1.00 kg, so 1 mg L⁻¹ ≈ 1 mass-ppm.

Percentages: chem-c02-q09, chem-c02-q14; ppm and ppb: chem-c02-q11.

pH and pOH

  • pH = −log [H₃O⁺], and back again [H₃O⁺] = 10^(−pH). pOH = −log [OH⁻]. At 298 K, pH + pOH = 14.00 (K_w = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0·10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K; Binas, ion product of water).
  • Strong acid: the acid ionises completely, so [H₃O⁺] equals the concentration of the acid (multiply by two for H₂SO₄ when it is treated as fully deprotonated). A strong base works the same way with [OH⁻]; check how many OH⁻ one formula unit gives (NaOH: 1; Ba(OH)₂: 2). See chem-c02-q03, chem-c02-q04.
  • Weak acids and bases do not ionise completely; their pH needs K_a (CCVX: K_z) or K_b and belongs to C05 — chemical equilibrium.
  • Significant figures for pH: a pH gets as many decimals as [H₃O⁺] has significant figures. For [H₃O⁺] = 2.5·10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ (two figures), pH = 2.60 (two decimals).

C2.2 Principles

Mass ratio

  • The numbers in u in a reaction equation can be read as grams, so masses scale in a fixed ratio. From Mg + S → MgS: 24.31 g Mg reacts with 32.06 g S to give 56.37 g MgS. Every sample of this reaction obeys that same ratio (law of constant composition).
  • This method is always allowed, but it only compares masses. The moment particles, volumes or concentrations enter the problem, work through moles.

Mole ratio and the five-step method

  • The coefficients of a balanced equation give the mole ratio. For 2 C₄H₁₀ + 13 O₂ → 8 CO₂ + 10 H₂O: n(C₄H₁₀)/2 = n(O₂)/13 = n(CO₂)/8 = n(H₂O)/10.
  • Systematic problem approach, five steps:
    1. Write the balanced equation.
    2. Convert the given substance to mol.
    3. State the mole ratio between given and asked.
    4. Compute the amount of the asked substance.
    5. Convert to the unit the question asks for.
  • Every conversion runs through the amount of substance:
mass m        ── ÷ M ──► ┐
gas volume    ── ÷ V_m ─►│ n (mol) ── × N_A ──► number of particles
solution vol. ── × c ───►│    └────── × M ────► mass of the asked substance
  • Do not use the mass ratio where the mole ratio belongs.

Volume ratio of gases

  • At the same T and p, equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of particles (Avogadro's law). For gases the volume ratio therefore equals the mole ratio from the equation: burning 1.0 L butane needs 13/2 × 1.0 = 6.5 L oxygen. See chem-c02-q06.

Excess and deficiency

  • A reactant is in excess when more of it is present than is needed for the other reactant; the other reactant is in deficiency. The reactant in deficiency runs out first and decides how much product forms.
  • If the question does not say which reactant is in deficiency, check: convert both amounts to mol and compare with the mole ratio. The one that comes up short is the deficiency. See chem-c02-q07.
  • A back-titration adds a known excess of one reactant and then measures what is left over with a second titration: reacted = added − left over. See chem-c02-q09.

Yield

  • Yield = actual output / theoretical output, as a fraction or × 100%. The theoretical output comes from a five-step calculation assuming complete conversion.
  • A yield below 100% means you need more starting material for a target amount: divide by the yield, never multiply. See chem-c02-q10.

Conservation of mass

  • In a closed reactor, total mass is conserved: whatever goes in must come out, reacted or not. Atoms are not created or destroyed, only rearranged. Conservation laws as such are treated in C03 — conservation laws and cycles.

Significant figures and exam verbs

  • Multiplying and dividing: give the answer in as many significant figures as the measurement with the fewest. Adding and subtracting: as many decimals as the measurement with the fewest decimals. Counted numbers and exact constants do not count. A logarithm gets as many decimals as the original value had significant figures (CCVX syllabus, domain A).
  • Rounding to significant figures only earns points when the question asks for it.
  • Do not round in intermediate steps; round only the final answer.
  • The verb "calculate" means: show the formulas or principles, the values used and the steps, and give the unit unless the question states it. A bare number without working earns little.

CCVX versus the Dutch syllabus

  • In both: everything above.
  • Dutch syllabus only: charge Q and the Faraday constant F = Q / n (CCVX does not list these).
  • CCVX only: the relative molecular mass M_r without a unit, and volume percentage, mass-ppm (mg kg⁻¹) and mass-ppb (μg kg⁻¹) spelled out explicitly.

questions.questionHtml: A vitamin tablet contains 500 mg of ascorbic acid (C₆H₈O₆). Calculate the amount, in mol, of ascorbic acid in one tablet.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. M(C₆H₈O₆) = 6 × 12.01 + 8 × 1.008 + 6 × 16.00 = 176.12 g mol⁻¹ (Binas, table of molar masses or atomic masses).
  2. Convert the mass: 500 mg = 0.500 g.
  3. n = m / M = 0.500 / 176.12 = 2.84·10⁻³ mol (three significant figures, as in 0.500 g).

questions.questionHtml: A lab technician dissolves 6.24 g of sodium sulfate (Na₂SO₄) in water and makes the volume up to 250.0 mL. Calculate the molarity of the Na⁺ ions in this solution.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. M(Na₂SO₄) = 2 × 22.99 + 32.06 + 4 × 16.00 = 142.04 g mol⁻¹.
  2. n(Na₂SO₄) = 6.24 / 142.04 = 4.39·10⁻² mol in 250.0 mL = 0.2500 L.
  3. c(Na₂SO₄) = 4.39·10⁻² / 0.2500 = 0.176 mol L⁻¹.
  4. Each Na₂SO₄ gives two Na⁺ ions: [Na⁺] = 2 × 0.176 = 0.351 mol L⁻¹ (three significant figures).

questions.questionHtml: Calculate the pH of a 0.0250 M solution of nitric acid (HNO₃) at 298 K.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Nitric acid is a strong acid (Binas, table 49): it ionises completely, so [H₃O⁺] = 0.0250 mol L⁻¹.
  2. pH = −log [H₃O⁺] = −log (0.0250) = 1.602.
  3. [H₃O⁺] has three significant figures, so the pH gets three decimals.

questions.questionHtml: 1.28 g of barium hydroxide octahydrate (Ba(OH)₂·8H₂O) is dissolved in water and made up to 400.0 mL at 298 K. Calculate the pH of this solution. Assume complete dissociation; Ba(OH)₂ is a strong base.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. M(Ba(OH)₂·8H₂O) = 137.33 + 2 × (16.00 + 1.008) + 8 × 18.016 = 315.5 g mol⁻¹ (adding the Binas table-99 atomic masses).
  2. n = m / M = 1.28 / 315.5 = 4.06·10⁻³ mol Ba(OH)₂.
  3. Each unit gives two OH⁻ ions: n(OH⁻) = 8.11·10⁻³ mol in 0.4000 L, so [OH⁻] = 2.03·10⁻² mol L⁻¹.
  4. pOH = −log (2.03·10⁻²) = 1.693; pH = 14.00 − 1.693 = 12.31.

questions.questionHtml: A blast furnace extracts iron from haematite: 2 Fe₂O₃ + 3 C → 4 Fe + 3 CO₂. A batch of ore has a mass of 1.00 tonne (1.00·10⁶ g) and consists of 92.0% Fe₂O₃ by mass. Carbon is present in excess. Calculate the maximum mass of iron that can form from this batch.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Mass of Fe₂O₃: 0.920 × 1.00·10⁶ = 9.20·10⁵ g.
  2. M(Fe₂O₃) = 2 × 55.85 + 3 × 16.00 = 159.7 g mol⁻¹, so n(Fe₂O₃) = 9.20·10⁵ / 159.7 = 5.76·10³ mol.
  3. Mole ratio Fe₂O₃ : Fe = 2 : 4 = 1 : 2, so n(Fe) = 2 × 5.76·10³ = 1.15·10⁴ mol.
  4. m(Fe) = n × M = 1.15·10⁴ × 55.85 = 6.43·10⁵ g = 643 kg (three significant figures, as in 92.0%).

questions.questionHtml: Butane burns completely: 2 C₄H₁₀ + 13 O₂ → 8 CO₂ + 10 H₂O(l). Calculate the volume of oxygen (in L) needed for the complete combustion of 5.00 L of butane, and the volume of carbon dioxide formed. All gas volumes are measured at 298 K and p = p₀.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. At the same T and p, gas volumes stand in the same ratio as the mole numbers (Avogadro's law), so V-ratios equal the coefficient ratios.
  2. V(O₂) = (13/2) × 5.00 = 32.5 L.
  3. V(CO₂) = (8/2) × 5.00 = 20.0 L.
  4. No V_m is needed because the volume ratio is used directly (water is liquid, so its volume is not asked).

questions.questionHtml: Aluminium and chlorine react: 2 Al + 3 Cl₂ → 2 AlCl₃. A chemist lets 5.40 g of aluminium react with 20.5 g of chlorine. Show which reactant is in deficiency, and calculate the mass of aluminium chloride that forms.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. n(Al) = 5.40 / 26.98 = 0.200 mol; n(Cl₂) = 20.5 / 70.90 = 0.289 mol.
  2. For 0.200 mol Al, the equation needs (3/2) × 0.200 = 0.300 mol Cl₂. Only 0.289 mol is available, so Cl₂ is in deficiency and decides the product amount.
  3. Mole ratio Cl₂ : AlCl₃ = 3 : 2, so n(AlCl₃) = (2/3) × 0.289 = 0.193 mol.
  4. M(AlCl₃) = 26.98 + 3 × 35.45 = 133.33 g mol⁻¹; m = 0.193 × 133.33 = 25.7 g (three significant figures).

questions.questionHtml: A 25.00 mL sample of a sodium hydroxide solution is titrated with 0.0985 M hydrochloric acid. The equivalence point occurs at 22.65 mL of acid. Calculate the molarity of the sodium hydroxide solution.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Reaction: OH⁻ + H₃O⁺ → 2 H₂O, so at the equivalence point n(OH⁻) = n(H₃O⁺).
  2. n(HCl) = 0.0985 mol L⁻¹ × 22.65·10⁻³ L = 2.231·10⁻³ mol.
  3. c(NaOH) = 2.231·10⁻³ / 25.00·10⁻³ = 8.92·10⁻² = 0.0892 mol L⁻¹ (three significant figures, as in 0.0985 and 22.65).

questions.questionHtml: An antacid tablet contains calcium carbonate. A tablet weighing 0.652 g is dissolved in 50.00 mL of 0.200 M hydrochloric acid (an excess). The excess acid is then titrated with 0.100 M sodium hydroxide, which takes 18.30 mL. The reaction in the tablet is CaCO₃ + 2 H₃O⁺ → Ca²⁺ + 3 H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the mass percentage of CaCO₃ in the tablet.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Added acid: n(H₃O⁺) = 0.200 × 50.00·10⁻³ = 1.00·10⁻² mol.
  2. Excess acid back-titrated: n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 18.30·10⁻³ = 1.830·10⁻³ mol, so n(H₃O⁺) left over = 1.830·10⁻³ mol.
  3. Reacted with CaCO₃: 1.00·10⁻² − 1.830·10⁻³ = 8.17·10⁻³ mol H₃O⁺.
  4. Mole ratio CaCO₃ : H₃O⁺ = 1 : 2, so n(CaCO₃) = 4.09·10⁻³ mol.
  5. M(CaCO₃) = 40.08 + 12.01 + 3 × 16.00 = 100.09 g mol⁻¹; m = 4.09·10⁻³ × 100.09 = 0.409 g.
  6. Mass percentage: 0.409 / 0.652 × 100% = 62.7% (three significant figures).

questions.questionHtml: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is made from salicylic acid and ethanoic anhydride: C₇H₆O₃ + C₄H₆O₃ → C₉H₈O₄ + C₂H₄O₂. A student starts with 4.10 g of salicylic acid and an excess of ethanoic anhydride, and isolates 4.61 g of aspirin after purification. Calculate the percentage yield.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. M(C₇H₆O₃) = 7 × 12.01 + 6 × 1.008 + 3 × 16.00 = 138.12 g mol⁻¹; M(C₉H₈O₄) = 180.15 g mol⁻¹.
  2. n(salicylic acid) = 4.10 / 138.12 = 2.97·10⁻² mol; the ratio is 1 : 1, so the theoretical amount of aspirin is the same.
  3. Theoretical mass: 2.97·10⁻² × 180.15 = 5.35 g.
  4. Yield = 4.61 / 5.35 × 100% = 86.2% (three significant figures).

questions.questionHtml: The guideline value for lead in drinking water is 10 μg per litre. Analysis of a 250.0 mL sample of tap water finds 3.5 μg of lead; the density of the sample is 1.00 kg L⁻¹. Express the measured lead concentration in mass-ppb (μg kg⁻¹) and in mass-ppm (mg kg⁻¹), and state whether the sample exceeds the guideline.
questions.answerHtml: 14 mass-ppb = 1.4·10⁻² mass-ppm; yes, it exceeds the guideline of 10 mass-ppb.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 250.0 mL of water has a mass of 0.2500 kg (density 1.00 kg L⁻¹).
  2. Concentration = 3.5 μg / 0.2500 kg = 14 μg kg⁻¹ = 14 mass-ppb.
  3. In mg kg⁻¹: 14 μg kg⁻¹ = 1.4·10⁻² mg kg⁻¹ = 1.4·10⁻² mass-ppm.
  4. 10 μg L⁻¹ corresponds to 10 μg kg⁻¹ = 10 mass-ppb, so 14 mass-ppb exceeds the guideline (two significant figures, as in 3.5 μg).

questions.questionHtml: Concentrated hydrochloric acid contains 37 mass% HCl and has a density of 1.19 g mL⁻¹. Calculate the molarity of concentrated hydrochloric acid.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Take 1.00 L = 1000 mL of the acid; its mass is 1000 × 1.19 = 1.19·10³ g.
  2. Of this, 37% is HCl: m(HCl) = 0.37 × 1.19·10³ = 4.4·10² g.
  3. M(HCl) = 36.46 g mol⁻¹, so n(HCl) = 4.4·10² / 36.46 = 12 mol.
  4. This is per litre, so the molarity is 12 mol L⁻¹ (two significant figures, as in 37%).

questions.questionHtml: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂. Calculate the volume of oxygen gas formed when 15.0 g of hydrogen peroxide decomposes completely, at 298 K and p = p₀.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. M(H₂O₂) = 2 × 1.008 + 2 × 16.00 = 34.02 g mol⁻¹; n = 15.0 / 34.02 = 0.441 mol.
  2. Mole ratio H₂O₂ : O₂ = 2 : 1, so n(O₂) = 0.441 / 2 = 0.220 mol (unrounded: 0.2205).
  3. V = n × V_m = 0.2205 × 24.5 = 5.40 L (three significant figures).

questions.questionHtml: A 1.000 g mixture of sodium chloride and potassium chloride is dissolved in water, and an excess of silver nitrate solution is added. All chloride precipitates as AgCl(s). The washed and dried precipitate weighs 2.147 g. Calculate the mass percentage of NaCl in the mixture.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. M(AgCl) = 107.87 + 35.45 = 143.32 g mol⁻¹, so n(AgCl) = 2.147 / 143.32 = 1.498·10⁻² mol.
  2. Let x = mass of NaCl in g; then the mass of KCl is (1.000 − x) g. Each mole of NaCl or KCl gives one mole of AgCl.
  3. n(AgCl) = x / 58.44 + (1.000 − x) / 74.55 = 1.498·10⁻² mol (M(NaCl) = 58.44, M(KCl) = 74.55 g mol⁻¹).
  4. Solving this linear equation: x × (1/58.44 − 1/74.55) = 1.498·10⁻² − 1.000/74.55, so x = (1.498·10⁻² − 1.341·10⁻²) / (1.711·10⁻² − 1.341·10⁻²) = 0.424 g.
  5. Mass percentage: 0.424 / 1.000 × 100% = 42.4% (three significant figures).
